headline: Rates Edge Lower in a Holiday Week Steered by Stock Swings
tileReason: The daily 30-year average ended at 7.29%, down from 7.33% a week earlier, as nervous investors bought bonds during a tech stock selloff.
takeaway:
Rates finished the holiday week a little lower. Mortgage News Daily's 30-year average ended Friday at 7.29%, down 0.04% from 7.33% the Friday before, after touching a two-week low of 7.26% on Wednesday. Friday's reading rose 0.03% in a short, thin session, and Freddie Mac's weekly survey, released a day early on Wednesday, fell to 7.21% from 7.28%.

Swings in tech stocks did most of the steering. Stocks surged Monday after Nvidia brought back Jensen Huang as CEO, then tech shares slid Tuesday and sharply early Wednesday, and nervous investors bought Treasury bonds for safety. That pushed the 10-year Treasury yield, which mortgage rates tend to follow, down eight trading days in a row to about 4.85% Wednesday, from 4.92% the Friday before. Stocks bounced back Friday and the 10-year rose to roughly 4.90% to 4.94% (sources differ, and an official close wasn't posted yet), which is why rates ticked up at the end of the week.

Strong economic news pushed the other way. Consumer confidence jumped to 103.3, far above forecasts, third-quarter growth was revised up to 4.3%, and first-time jobless claims fell to 189,000. The Fed's preferred inflation gauge, PCE, rose 3.8% from a year earlier in October, and the core version that leaves out food and energy came in at 3.3%, a tenth above forecasts; normally that combination lifts rates, but this week bonds mostly looked past it.

Lenders still have room to cut. Mortgage rates sit unusually far above Treasuries: the Optimal Blue index, which tracks rates borrowers actually lock, was about 2.19% above the 10-year on Nov 17, the latest day recorded, versus a long-run average of about 1.76%. Buyers noticed the lower rates, too: mortgage applications rose 6.1% in the week ending Nov 20, with purchase applications up 10%, according to the Mortgage Bankers Association.

A December Fed hike now looks all but certain. Futures markets, where traders bet on the Fed's next move, put the odds of a quarter-point increase in the Fed's short-term rate on Dec 9 at about 99% Friday, up from roughly 91% to 96% Monday, after New York Fed President John Williams said he wouldn't rule out hikes at back-to-back meetings. Markets also see roughly a 59% chance of another increase in January; these are market expectations, not a Fed forecast.

Next week's jobs report is the big test. October job openings come Tuesday and the November jobs report arrives Friday, Dec 4, the last major reading before the Fed meets; a soft report could help rates extend this month's improvement, while a strong one could push them back up. Monday's 30-day outlook leaned toward rates staying within about 0.125% of 7.33%, and so far they have, at 7.29%.

drivers.title: Tech stock selloff sent money into bonds
drivers.text: Tech shares fell Tuesday and sharply early Wednesday, with the Nasdaq down as much as about 4.6% before recovering part of the loss. Nervous investors bought Treasuries for safety, the 10-year yield fell eight straight trading days to about 4.85%, and the daily 30-year average dropped to a two-week low of 7.26% Wednesday.

drivers.title: Strong economy and slightly hot core inflation
drivers.text: Consumer confidence surged to 103.3, third-quarter growth was revised up to 4.3%, jobless claims fell to 189,000, and October core PCE inflation rose 3.3% from a year earlier, a tenth above forecasts. A strong economy and sticky inflation usually hold rates up, which kept this week's drop small.

drivers.title: December Fed hike all but locked in
drivers.text: After Williams said he wouldn't rule out back-to-back hikes, futures odds of a quarter-point hike on Dec 9 climbed to about 99% by Friday, with about a 59% chance of another in January. When investors expect the Fed to keep raising its short-term rate, longer-term yields and mortgage rates have a hard time falling far.

drivers.title: Oil fell to a three-month low
drivers.text: U.S. crude dropped almost 4% Monday to about $80 a barrel, its lowest close since late August. Cheaper energy eases inflation worries, which helped bonds hold steady even as stocks soared that day.

drivers.title: Friday's stock rebound lifted yields
drivers.text: Stocks jumped Friday as chip and AI shares bounced back, and investors sold some of the Treasuries they had bought for safety. The 10-year rose to roughly 4.90% to 4.94%, and the daily 30-year average edged up 0.03% to 7.29% in the short holiday session.

talkingPoints.buyers: Rates ended the week near a two-week low, with the daily 30-year average at 7.29% and Freddie Mac's survey at 7.21%. Next Friday's jobs report could move rates a meaningful amount in either direction, so buyers close to a contract may want to talk with Stuart about how a quarter-point swing would change their payment and what their timeline allows.
talkingPoints.sellers: Lower rates this month are bringing buyers back: purchase mortgage applications rose 10% in the week ending Nov 20. Rates are still above 7%, so pricing and concessions still matter; talk with Stuart about how a seller-paid rate buydown compares with a price cut for your buyers.
talkingPoints.oneLiner: Rates dipped slightly this holiday week to about 7.29% as tech stock swings pushed money into bonds, and next Friday's jobs report is the next big test.
